title: Psalm 104: The Creator Who Feeds Every Creature
summary: A hymn of wonder at God the Creator. Clothed in light, he stretches out the heavens like a tent, sets the earth on its foundations, drives back the waters, and sends springs to water the valleys. He feeds wild donkeys, birds, cattle, lions, and people, marks the seasons with the moon, and fills the sea with creatures, even Leviathan. All living things depend on him for food and breath, and when he sends his Spirit they are created. The psalmist vows to sing to God all his life and prays that sinners vanish from the earth.
story: Psalm 104 is the twin of Psalm 103. Both begin and end with “Bless the LORD, O my soul”, but where Psalm 103 praised God's mercy to Israel, Psalm 104 praises his care for the whole created world. It retells creation in roughly the order of Genesis 1: light, the heavens, the waters, the dry land, vegetation, the moon and sun, the sea creatures, and humanity at work. After two psalms focused on human frailty and forgiveness, this one reminds the reader that God's kingship, celebrated through Book IV, extends over every creature. The following two psalms will turn to Israel's history, so Psalm 104 sets that history against the widest possible background.
historical:
The psalm has no heading in Hebrew; the Septuagint attributes it to David. Its date is unknown, and scholars have proposed settings from the monarchy to after the exile. The psalm is most often discussed alongside the Great Hymn to the Aten, an Egyptian hymn from the reign of Pharaoh Akhenaten in the fourteenth century BC, which praises the sun disk for bringing daylight after dangerous night, sending people to their work, caring for animals and birds, and giving life to the fish in the river and the ships on the waters. Several sections of Psalm 104, especially verses 20 to 30, follow a similar sequence. Scholars differ on the relationship: some think Israelite poets knew a form of the Egyptian hymn, perhaps through Canaanite channels; others think both drew on a shared tradition of praising the creator's care; still others doubt any direct link.

Whatever the connection, the difference is decisive. In the Egyptian hymn, the sun is the god. In Psalm 104, the sun is a creature that knows when to set (verse 19), and both night and day belong to the LORD who made them.
cultural:
The psalm pictures the world as ancient Israel experienced it. The heavens are a tent stretched over the earth, and God's upper rooms sit above the waters over the sky. The earth rests on foundations, and the deep, the primeval waters, once covered it until God rebuked them and set a boundary. Neighboring peoples told stories of gods fighting the sea; here the waters simply flee at God's thunder. Leviathan, a sea monster that Canaanite texts from Ugarit describe as a chaos dragon, appears in verse 26 as a creature God formed to play in the sea.

The details of land and life are those of the Levant. Springs in the valleys and rain on the mountains were the difference between life and death in a land without great rivers. Wine, oil, and bread (verse 15) were the three staple products of Israel's agriculture. The cedars of Lebanon were famous across the ancient world. Wild goats and rock badgers (the hyrax, a small animal that lives among rocks) live on the high crags, and lions hunt at night. Humans go out to work at dawn and come home in the evening, one creature among many in the daily rhythm God has set.
literary: The psalm is a long, carefully ordered hymn that moves through creation in stages. Verses 1 to 4 describe God's majesty in the heavens; verses 5 to 9 the founding of the earth and taming of the waters; verses 10 to 18 the provision of water and food for animals, birds, and people; verses 19 to 23 the rhythm of moon, sun, night, and day; verses 24 to 26 the sea. Verses 27 to 30 draw the theme together: every creature looks to God for food and breath. Verses 31 to 35 conclude with prayer and praise. The speaker alternates between speaking about God and to him. The exclamation of verse 24, “How many are Your works, O LORD”, is the psalm's center of gravity.

outline.t: Clothed in light: the Creator's majesty
The earth founded and the waters bounded
Springs, food, and homes for every creature
Moon, sun, night, and the day's work
The sea and its creatures, Leviathan at play
All creatures look to God for food and breath
May God rejoice in his works; I will sing all my life

doctrines.note: God did not only make the world; he keeps it. The psalm describes creation as ongoing care: he waters the mountains, makes grass grow, gives food in due season, and renews the face of the earth.

Every creature, from young lions to people, depends on God for food, life, and breath. When he opens his hand, they are satisfied; when he takes away their breath, they die. Nothing in the world is self-sufficient.
“In wisdom You have made them all” (verse 24). The order and variety of the world reflect God's wisdom, which is why studying creation can lead to praise.
“When You send Your Spirit, they are created” (verse 30). The Hebrew ruach means breath, wind, and spirit, and here it is God's life-giving power in every living thing.

words.note: Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. The psalm plays on its range: God makes the winds his messengers (verse 4), takes away creatures' breath (verse 29), and sends his Spirit to create (verse 30). The same word appears in Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God hovers over the waters.

Chokmah, wisdom, the skill of a craftsman as well as the insight of a sage. Proverbs 3:19 and 8:22-31 also describe God founding the earth by wisdom. Here wisdom is visible in the fitting of each creature to its place.

Liviathan, Leviathan. In Canaanite myth and in some Old Testament poetry (Isaiah 27:1), a fearsome sea monster. In this psalm it is a creature God formed to frolic in the sea, a deliberate shrinking of the ancient chaos monster to a plaything in God's world.
Chadash, to renew. In verse 30 God renews the face of the ground. Creation is not a finished object left to run down; God keeps making it new, generation after generation.

christ: Hebrews 1:7 quotes verse 4, in its Greek form, to speak of God's angels as servants, contrasting them with the Son, through whom God made the world (Hebrews 1:2). The New Testament names Christ as the one through whom all things were made and in whom all things hold together (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16-17), so Christians read this psalm's Creator and sustainer as the triune God, with the Son and the Spirit active in the making and keeping of the world. Jesus' teaching that the Father feeds the birds of the air and clothes the grass of the field (Matthew 6:26-30) breathes the same air as this psalm. And the renewing of the face of the earth by God's Spirit points toward the new creation that the New Testament hopes for (Romans 8:19-23; Revelation 21:1).

hard.q: Why does a joyful creation hymn end with a prayer that sinners vanish from the earth?
hard.a: After thirty-four verses of wonder, verse 35 can sound like a sour note. But it follows from what the psalm has said. If the whole world is God's good work, sustained by his hand and meant for his joy, then human wickedness is the one thing that spoils it. The prayer is for the removal of evil from God's creation rather than a private wish for revenge, and it is prayed to God rather than carried out by the psalmist. Some interpreters read it as a prayer that sin itself come to an end, others as a prayer for judgment on the unrepentant. The New Testament shares the hope that nothing evil will remain in the renewed creation while also holding out the call for sinners to turn and live.

questions: The psalm finds God in springs, cedars, rock badgers, and lions. What parts of the natural world most often lead you to praise, and which do you overlook?
Verse 23 places human work within the same daily rhythm as the animals'. How does that change the way you think about your own labor?
If every breath depends on God's Spirit, what would it mean to live today as a creature rather than as someone self-sufficient?
